title: Fixed relative shifts reversed the Ob-Yenisey mean peak excess in 31 certified years from 1980 to 2011
abstract: We tested whether the published same-year excess in the mean seven-day peak of summed Ob and Yenisey gauge flow survives relative timing shifts. We used ArcticGRO v20261104 and the same 31 certified years from 1980 to 2011 as prior work. We kept Ob fixed and shifted Yenisey by each integer from -30 to +30 days. The exact excess over independent year pairing within three periods ranged from -1.24% at -19 days to +1.27% at -3 days. Zero delay gave +1.04%. The earlier code used four groups rather than its stated three groups; that rule gave +0.80%. The positive excess did not survive all shifts, including shifts within 14 days. A test across all 61 shifts gave p = 0.0093; its strongest departure was negative. The zero-delay family-adjusted p was 0.0831. Five-year pairing and equal seasonal volume also gave both signs. These shifts are a diagnostic range, not measured travel times. The result shows that the sign of this gauge index depends on timing assumptions. It does not estimate coastal freshwater arrival or show a physical cause. Short records, regulation, source error and year-exchangeability assumptions limit the test. The package includes code, source hashes, aggregate curves, null draws, a numerical audit and a figure. Raw data remain external.

display.caption: The same-year peak excess changes sign across fixed timing shifts. The lower panel compares pointwise and 61-shift family-adjusted tests. A positive delay moves Yenisey later; Ob stays fixed. These are gauge indices, not observed coastal flows.

citations.reason: Its pair result and travel-time limit set this question. We use the same sample and new code. Its code uses four groups rather than the three stated in its text.
Prior three-river dependence test provides context; no code is reused.
